title: Complexity analysis of a trust funnel algorithm for equality constrained optimization
contribution: A trust-funnel phase 1 for equality-constrained optimization that seeks objective decrease while reaching eps-feasibility and keeps the O(eps^-3/2) complexity of Cartis-Gould-Toint's two-phase ARC method, plus a TRACE-based phase 2 with the same complexity (read as arXiv v1; Theorem 36 p. 25, Appendix A pp. 30-35).
problem_entry: Rival with the right bound but a nameable defect: the two-phase ARC method [8] whose phase 1 entirely ignores the objective, a departure from SQP practice that seeks feasibility and optimality together (Abstract; pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Keep the two-phase structure but make phase 1 a trust funnel (normal step on 0.5||c||^2, tangential step in Null(J)) with TRACE acceptance (decrease/||s||^3) and lambda/||n|| ratio control; F- vs V-iterations chosen by conditions (15a)-(15f); tangential step discarded if (14) fails (pp. 3-8).
assumptions: f, c in C^2 (A1, p. 2); iterates in compact set, H_k bounded (A2, p. 7); Lipschitz Hessians of v and f on the path (A22, p. 18); bound is on ||J^T c||, on ||c|| only under full rank (Cor. 37, p. 25); (15e)-(15f) admitted as needed for complexity (p. 6); code sets kappa_ht = kappa_hs = 1e20 (Table 1, p. 27).
proof_devices: index-set partition F/V and S/C/E (Lemma 3, p. 8)
monotone funnel radius v_max as upper bound on v (Lemma 6, pp. 10-11) with decrease >= kappa_rho(1-kappa_v2)||s||^3 per success (Lemma 7, pp. 11-12)
finite termination by contradiction on |I| = infinity (Lemmas 16-20, Theorem 21, pp. 15-18)
step-norm lower bounds from lambda/||n|| <= sigma-bar ratio control (Lemmas 25-26, pp. 20-21)
at most one V-expansion between successes (Lemma 13, p. 14) and constant-factor growth of a critical ratio after contractions (Lemmas 29-30, 33-35, pp. 22-25)
product bound K(eps) = 1 + (K_sigma + K_Delta)(K_C^v + 1)K_C^f = O(eps^-3/2) (Theorem 36, p. 25)
tolerance coupling eps = eps_feas * eps_inf giving feasibility or infeasible stationarity (pp. 25-26)
lemma-by-lemma transfer of [8] and TRACE [15] results to a TRACE-based target-following phase 2 (Lemmas 39-46, Theorem 47, pp. 30-35)
experiments: Matlab; TF vs TF-V-only (same code with tangential step forced to zero, same phase-2 trust funnel, subproblems solved accurately) on CUTEst equality problems 190 -> 33 with named removals plus an uncounted one-hour 'neither terminated' filter (60 by subtraction); metrics #V, #F, f and dual infeasibility after phase 1, phase-2 iterations (Table 2, pp. 26-28); TF losses (BT5, HS27) not discussed.
positioning: Continues and corrects Cartis-Gould-Toint's two-phase ARC [8], borrowing TRACE [15] and the Gould-Toint trust funnel [21]; claims parity of complexity, framed as 'a next step' (pp. 2, 28).
writing: Contribution sentence in the abstract; one-line plain previews before each lemma; 47 numbered results vs one experiment table; moderate hedging ('typically', 'We do not claim ... guarantees', pp. 26, 28).
limits_future: Stated: complexity for ||J^T c|| unless full rank (p. 25); the phase 2 used in experiments has no complexity guarantee (p. 26). Unstated: the tested configuration differs from the analysed one, no comparison with SQP codes or with [8]; no future work in the conclusion (p. 28).

method_links.note: Two-phase architecture kept for complexity; steering (F vs V iterations, funnel-radius updates) happens only inside phase 1; in tension with Taste 3.

The premise that complexity-minded design improves practice (stated for convex) organizes the paper; practical value is checked only against an ablated copy; complexity-only conditions made near-inactive in code (inference). Contrasts with his later warning that better complexity has not meant better performance.
Feasibility-only rival built in the same code by switching off one component, with identical phase 2 and subproblem accuracy; incumbent wins (BT5, HS27) not named in the text.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Keep a practical framework (trust funnel) and add only the acceptance/ratio tests that carry the complexity proof, delegating proofs to the source lemmas of TRACE one by one.

transferable: Count successes through a monotone funnel quantity decreasing by >= kappa||s||^3 per success, then multiply by a constant bound on failures between successes (Lemmas 7, 13, 30, 35; Theorem 36, pp. 11-12, 14, 22-25).
Set the phase-1 tolerance eps = eps_feas * eps_inf so one stopping test certifies feasibility or infeasible stationarity (pp. 25-26).
Test the contribution with a one-switch ablation of your own code (tangential step forced to zero), holding phase 2 and subproblem accuracy fixed (pp. 26-27).
Allow a computed sub-step to be discarded when explicit compatibility tests fail, so the analysis sees only steps satisfying them (p. 5).

quotes.text: This is due to the fact that, at least for convex optimization, algorithms designed with complexity bounds in mind have led to methods with improved practical performance.
However, we find this idea to be unsatisfactory since such an approach would entirely ignore the objective function.

title: A sequential algorithm for solving nonlinear optimization problems with chance constraints
contribution: An Sl1QP-style trust-region method for cardinality-constrained nonlinear problems (SAA of chance constraints) built on a new exact penalty, the minimum over scenario selections of l1 penalties, with MIQP subproblems over only the eps-critical selections, a global convergence proof to penalty stationarity, and a Matlab/Cplex prototype on a 2-D example and a cash-flow problem (pp. 4-26).
problem_entry: Chance-constrained problems via SAA give |{i: c_i(x) <= 0}| >= M; convex approximations are conservative, MINLP may be intractable, MPCC reformulations can stall at spurious points, Luedtke's MILP methods are linear only; local search with a stationarity guarantee is accepted on purpose (pp. 1-4).
key_idea: Exact penalty phi = rho f + <<c>>_M with <<w>>_M = min over size-M selections of l1 violation (= min_S phi_S); trust-region subproblem minimizes min over S in S_{M,k} of convex piecewise-quadratic models, with S_{M,k} containing at least the eps-critical selections; M = N recovers Sl1QP (pp. 4-11).
assumptions: f, c_i Lipschitz with Lipschitz gradients on a bounded convex set containing the iterates, H_k bounded (A4, p. 10) and PSD (p. 8); rho and eps fixed (p. 8); CQ per critical selection for Lemma 3 (pp. 7-8); equal-probability scenarios (p. 3).
proof_devices: local-minimizer equivalence of phi and all critical phi_S by finiteness and continuity (Lemma 1, pp. 6-7)
exact-penalty correspondence with (P) and with the violation measure (Lemmas 2-3, pp. 7-8)
criticality measure chi = max over critical S of classical l1 measures chi_S (eq. 20, Lemma 5, pp. 10-11)
SLQP-style global convergence following Byrd-Gould-Nocedal-Waltz [12]: Cauchy point per selection (Lemmas 10-11, pp. 12-13)
radius bounded below near non-stationary points via the TR reset delta_reset (Lemma 13, pp. 14-15)
summation contradiction for limit points (proof of Theorem 6, pp. 15-16)
local argument that a nearby better minimizer is accepted when (rho L_f + L_c + H_max) delta^2 is small (section 4.2, pp. 16-17)
experiments: Matlab R2015b + Cplex 12.6.2 big-M MIQP with disclosed heavy tuning and a 300 s limit (pp. 17-19); 2-D example with N = 5000, nine starts incl. a planted bad local minimizer, grid over rho and gamma (Tables 1-2, pp. 20-21); cash-flow problem (75 options, 20 periods, 5 random instances, N 100-5000, gamma 0.001-1) started at the robust solution, geometric means, relative improvement over robust (Tables 3-4, pp. 23-26); failures blamed on the subproblem solve (p. 24); global solvers tried at referee request, no numbers (footnote, p. 26).
positioning: Extends Luedtke et al.'s linear chance-constrained ideas to nonlinear problems and Fletcher's Sl1QP to cardinality constraints; rivals (convex approximations, MINLP, MPCC regularization) characterized but not run (pp. 2-4, 8, 11).
writing: Contribution in the first sentence of section 1; scope limit (stationarity only) stated in the introduction; 'we claim'/'we stress' hedges; non-proof section 4.2 on poor minimizers later tested by experiments; failures framed as not the algorithm's fault (pp. 1, 3, 16-17, 24).
limits_future: Fixed rho needs an update rule and, unlike standard NLP, a too-small rho hurts solution quality (p. 26); big-M Cplex MIQP too slow, Luedtke branch-and-cut proposed (pp. 18, 26-27); scenario sampling for CCP left open (p. 4); recourse via implicit z_i => x in P_i (p. 27).

method_links.note: Penalty parameter fixed; the conclusion names a steering rule as missing, and the experiments show rho decides which local minimizer is reached, not only speed.

Outer convergence theory dictates the minimum content of the inner MIQP (eps-critical selections); the rest is a cost-quality knob gamma; time-limited Cplex incumbents used as steps are outside the theory.
A hard case is planted (start at a poor local minimizer x_bad) to test the section 4.2 claim, on a 2-D toy rather than a transformed test set.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: M = N turns the cardinality penalty into the l1 penalty and Algorithm 3.1 into standard Sl1QP with its known convergence (Remark 8); keep-the-skeleton design in a combinatorial setting.

transferable: Define a combinatorial exact penalty as the minimum over scenario selections of classical l1 penalties and prove local-minimizer equivalence selection by selection (eqs. 1, 6, 8; Lemma 1, pp. 4-7).

Include in the subproblem only the eps-critical part of the combinatorial structure needed by the proof, expose the rest as a scale-free fraction gamma, and tabulate quality vs time over gamma (pp. 8-10, 19-20; Table 3, p. 25).
Add a trust-region reset value after each successful step to obtain the radius-bounded-below lemma (Lemma 13, pp. 14-15).
Plant a known bad starting point in a small example and grid the two key parameters to see whether the method escapes (Tables 1-2, pp. 20-21).
Initialize at the robust (all-constraints) solution and report improvement relative to it, averaged only over instances solved under every setting (pp. 23-24).

quotes.text: We emphasize that these outcomes do not represent a failure of the proposed algorithm, but rather are a consequence of the inefficient manner in which we are solving the subproblems
This is in contrast to standard nonlinear optimization, where a small value usually affects only the convergence speed, not the quality of the solution.

title: Concise complexity analyses for trust region methods
contribution: Short complexity proofs for trust-region methods whose radius is tied to ||g_k|| (O(eps_g^-2)) or, with a new update, to |lambda_k-| (O(max{eps_g^-2, eps_H^-3})), plus a fixed-radius O(eps^-3/2) variant whose practical costs are spelled out (read as arXiv v1; pp. 2-10).
problem_entry: Results exist inside general frameworks (Fan-Yuan, Grapiglia-Yuan-Yuan, Toint); the paper isolates the simplest instance to show the essential components, adds a second-order update, and contrasts with a better-complexity strategy (p. 2).
key_idea: Radius delta_k = gamma_k ||g_k|| or gamma_k |lambda_k-| (when ||g||^2 < |lambda-|^3), adapting only gamma_k; Cauchy decrease along -g or the leftmost eigenvector suffices; fixed radius sqrt(eps)/beta with exact solves for O(eps^-3/2) (pp. 3-9).
assumptions: f in C^2 with L-Lipschitz Hessian, bounded below (A1.1, p. 2); ||H_k|| <= kappa on iterates (A2.1, p. 4); exact leftmost eigenpair used, its cost not discussed (pp. 2-3); the fixed-radius method needs beta = L/2 and exact subproblem solutions (p. 9).
proof_devices: Cauchy decrease proportional to ||g||^2 or |lambda-|^3 because the radius is (Lemma 2.2, p. 4)
model error bound kappa gamma^2 ||g||^2 or (L/6) gamma^3 |lambda-|^3 (Lemma 2.3, p. 5)
induction lower bound gamma_min on the radius coefficient (Lemma 2.4, p. 5)
log bound on consecutive unsuccessful iterations independent of the radius rule (Lemma 2.6, p. 6)
telescoping f0 - f_inf over successes, multiplied by the failure bound (Theorems 2.9, 2.12, pp. 6-8)
two-case split on the trust-region multiplier xi_k vs sqrt(eps) for the fixed-radius method, after Ye's lecture notes (pp. 8-9)
direct lim ||g_k|| = 0 without a liminf-first argument (p. 10)
positioning: Openly a special case of [5, 6, 8] with simpler proofs; cites ARC and his own TRACE and inexact regularized Newton framework as O(eps^-3/2) methods; credits Ye's notes (pp. 2, 8, 10).
writing: Contributions immediately on p. 1; each strategy followed by a practical discussion (compatibility with the traditional update using typical values, p. 7; four costs of the better-complexity method, p. 9); open question stated plainly (p. 10); minor slips (Theorem 2.11 for Lemma 2.11, undefined K, pp. 8, 10).
limits_future: No analysis for the traditional radius update (p. 10); the O(eps^-3/2) fixed-radius method needs L, exact solves, eps fixed in advance and takes tiny steps (p. 9); eigenpair cost unaddressed (p. 3).

method_links.note: Section 2.5 asks what the better complexity class costs and concludes the O(eps^-3/2) method would likely behave very poorly in practice versus the O(eps^-2) strategies; an early written instance of Taste warning 3, contrasting with S026's premise.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Strip a known general framework to the simplest instance that still yields the bound in order to expose the essential algorithm components.

transferable: Three-lemma complexity template: decrease proportional to measure^p on successes; induction lower bound on the radius coefficient; log bound on consecutive failures; then telescope (Lemmas 2.2-2.8, pp. 4-8).
Tie the trust-region radius to the stationarity measure being driven to zero and adapt only its coefficient (Updates 2.7, 2.10, pp. 6-7).
Show exactly when a non-standard radius rule differs from the traditional one, using typical parameter values (p. 7).
Close any better-complexity variant with an explicit list of its practical costs (p. 9).

quotes.text: This would likely lead to very poor behavior in practice compared to the strategies in Sections 2.3 and 2.4, which are much less conservative.
It is unclear how to establish similar complexity results when a traditional trust region radius update is used.

title: R-Linear Convergence of Limited Memory Steepest Descent
contribution: Proves that Fletcher's limited memory steepest descent method converges R-linearly on strongly convex quadratics for any history length m, extending Dai-Liao's m = 1 (BB) result, with spectrum-designed illustrations (read as COR@L TR 16T-010 / arXiv v1; Theorem 3.12, pp. 13-14).
problem_entry: The rate of LMSD for m > 1 had not been analyzed, although BB (m = 1) was known to be R-linear and LMSD known to converge (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: No new algorithm: extend the Dai-Liao eigencomponent proof by linking Ritz values of T_k to the gradient weights (theta = c^T Lambda c, ||c|| = 1) and inducting over eigencomponents with k-independent cycle counts (pp. 6-14).
assumptions: Strongly convex quadratic with r distinct eigenvalues (A2.1, p. 4); no finite termination and G_k of full column rank with ||R_k^-1|| <= rho ||g_{k,1}||^-1 (A3.4, p. 8), adopted because variable-length cycles would be 'extremely cumbersome' (pp. 5-6).
proof_devices: eigenbasis weights with recursion d_{k,j+1,i} = (1 - alpha lambda_i) d_{k,j,i} (Lemma 2.3, p. 6)
finite termination once all reciprocal eigenvalues are used as stepsizes (Theorem 2.4, pp. 6-7)
Cauchy interlacing bounds on Ritz values (Lemma 3.5, p. 8)
theta_{k,j} = c^T Lambda c with ||c|| = 1 linking Ritz values to weights (Lemma 3.6, p. 8)
per-component contraction constants Delta_i with Delta_1 < 1 (Lemmas 3.7-3.8, pp. 9-10)
induction over components with k-independent cycle counts (Lemmas 3.9-3.10, pp. 10-13)
halving in K cycles, then R-linear constants c1 = 2 Delta^(K-1), c2 = 2^(-1/K) (Lemma 3.11, Theorem 3.12, pp. 13-14)
experiments: Matlab, five n = 100 quadratics designed by spectrum (incl. a Q-linear case lambda_n < 2 lambda_1), m = 1 and 5, eps = 1e-8, random initial stepsizes; outer/inner iteration counts (Table 1, p. 15) and plots of the proof's own weights |d_{k,j,i}| and constants Delta_i (Figs. 1-10, pp. 15-19); illustration only, choice of m out of scope (p. 14).
positioning: Extends Fletcher [3] and Dai-Liao [2] (with Raydan [5]); five references only (pp. 3, 19).
writing: Limits the practical reach of the theorem up front (p. 3); proofs borrowed from the m = 1 case flagged 'for completeness' (p. 13); the introduction promises a closing discussion of why practice beats theory that the brief conclusion does not contain (pp. 3, 19).
limits_future: Quadratics only; full-rank G_k assumed though column dropping is advocated, with a conjecture that the rate survives it (pp. 5-6, 8); theory does not explain the better observed behaviour (p. 3); no future work listed (p. 19).

method_links.note: States before the theorem that the proved rate does not capture practical behaviour; experiments framed to show where practice beats the bound.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Experiments display the internal objects of the analysis (eigen-weights per component, contraction constants coloured < 1 or >= 1) rather than only convergence curves.
The analysis bound ||R_k^-1|| <= rho ||g_{k,1}||^-1 is recast as a computable test for dropping old gradient columns (links to Heuristic 1).

transferable: To extend an m = 1 proof to a cycle/block method, keep its skeleton and add one lemma tying the block quantities (Ritz values) to the same eigen-weights (Lemma 3.6, p. 8).
Design synthetic tests by the structural property the proof depends on (spectrum), including a case where a stronger result holds (pp. 14-15).
Plot the analysis quantities themselves next to iteration counts (pp. 15-19).
When an assumption is adopted for tractability, give a practical rule based on its violations and state the conjecture that the result survives it (Remark 2.2, pp. 5-6).

quotes.text: Based on such evidence, we do not claim that the convergence results proved in this paper fully capture the practical behavior of LMSD methods.
It is not our goal to show the performance of Algorithm LMSD for various values of m, say to argue whether the performance improves or not as m is increased.
